chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ismail ibn Marrar, from Yunus, from some of his men, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

'The minimum of the purity (tuhr) is ten days. That is because a woman, at the beginning of her menstruation (haydh), may have abundant blood, so her menstruation may last ten days. It continually decreases as she gets older until it returns to three days. When it returns to three days, her menstruation is lifted (she reaches menopause), and it will not be less than three days. When a woman sees blood during her days of menstruation, she must leave salat. If the blood continues for three days, she is menstruating. If the blood stops after she has seen it for a day or two days, she performs ghusl and prays salat, and waits from the day she saw the blood until ten days. If she sees blood during those ten days from the day she first saw blood, for a day or two days until three days are completed for her, then what she saw at the beginning together with what she sees after that during the ten days is from menstruation.

If ten days pass from the day she first saw the blood and she does not see blood, then that day and the two days when she saw it were not from menstruation; rather it was from an illness — either from an ulcer in her abdomen or from internal causes. She must repeat the salat for those two days which she had abandoned, because she was not menstruating, and it is obligatory for her to make up what she missed of salat during the day and the two days.

If three days are completed for her, it is menstruation, and it is the minimum of menstruation, and make-up is not obligatory upon her. The purity will not be less than ten days. When a woman menstruates and her menstruation is five days and then the blood stops, she performs ghusl and prays salat. If she sees blood after that before ten days from the day of her purification are completed, that is from menstruation — she leaves salat. If she sees the blood secondly from when she first saw the second occurrence, completing ten days, and it continues upon her, she counts from the first blood she saw and the second — ten days — and then she is a mustahazah (one with irregular bleeding) and does what the mustahazah does.

And he (peace be upon him) said: 'Everything a woman sees during her days of menstruation — whether yellow or red — is from menstruation, and everything she sees after her days of menstruation is not from menstruation.'

key_terms.اغْتَسَلَتْ: ightasalat — she performed ghusl (ritual bath), required to regain purity
key_terms.الصَّلَاةَ: salat — ritual prayer; must be abandoned during haydh
key_terms.الطُّهْرِ: tuhr — the purity period between two menstrual cycles
key_terms.الْحَيْضِ: haydh — menstruation; the state of ritual impurity during the menstrual period
key_terms.الْقَضَاءُ: qada' — make-up of missed prayers; not required if haydh is confirmed
key_terms.الْمُسْتَحَاضَةُ: mustahazah — a woman with irregular bleeding (istihazah), subject to different rulings from haydh

ai.seo_question: What is the minimum purity period and minimum menstruation according to Imam al-Sadiq in Al-Kafi?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes the foundational jurisprudential rules for haydh (menstruation) and tuhr (purity period) in Shia Islamic law. The Imam specifies that the minimum purity period between cycles is ten days and the minimum haydh is three days, and provides detailed case-by-case rulings for intermittent or irregular bleeding, including when prayers must be abandoned and when they must be made up. This comprehensive legal framework has been central to Shia fiqh on women's ritual purity for over twelve centuries.
